chunks: What a module is in RTL. The question: What is a module?
In RTL (the code that describes digital hardware), a module is a named building block with a defined boundary.
It has ports for inputs and outputs, and a body that describes what is inside, either logic (gates and wires) or copies of other modules.
You write a module once and place as many copies as you need. Each copy is separate hardware that runs all the time, in parallel.
A module is not a software function that gets called.
Think of a cookie cutter and cookies. The module definition is the cutter, and every place you use it makes a new cookie, which is an instance.
Two instances means two physical copies of the circuit, each with its own wires. Like Lego, small blocks go into larger blocks, which go into the whole chip.
The cutter picture misses one thing: instances can be tuned with settings such as width.
From outside you see only the ports: inputs a and b, outputs s and c. The body (an XOR and an AND here) could change as long as the functionality and timing contract hold.
Port: a named input or output on a module's boundary, with a direction. Instance: one placed copy of a module, with its own name.
Hierarchy: modules containing other modules, forming a tree from the top level down. Parameter: a setting chosen when you place an instance, such as bus width.
Named connection: wiring a port by its name, as in . a(x) , rather than by position.
Write a half adder module (a circuit that adds two single bits) once.
It has inputs a and b, and outputs sum a b (1 when exactly one input is 1) and carry a times b (1 when both are).
A full adder then places two half-adder instances, named u ha1 and u ha2 , and adds one OR gate to combine the carries. The hardware holds two separate half adders.
Counting gates, each full adder uses 2 plus 2 plus 1 equals 5 , so a 32-bit adder built from a chain of 32 of them uses 160. That is the whole idea.
"A module is the basic design unit in Verilog or SystemVerilog: a named block with ports for its inputs and outputs, and a body containing logic or instances of other modules.
You write it once as a template and instantiate it as many times as you like, and each instance is separate hardware running in parallel, unlike a software function call.
Modules give you hierarchy, so teams can split a chip into blocks, test each one alone, and reuse them. In VHDL the equivalent is an entity with an architecture."
